# SK3540 — A `Dispose` method the type never declares

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

The type declares a public parameterless `Dispose()` that releases resources and does not implement `IDisposable`, so nothing the language or the framework does will ever call it.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Lifetime |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, review it |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |
| Supersedes | S2953 |

## Why

The cleanup is already written. It is public, it is spelled the way the framework spells it, and the base list does not say so — which means `using` will not bind to it, `is IDisposable` is false, a DI container's teardown walks past it, and every reviewer who sees the method assumes the release happens. This is the failure that looks finished from every angle except the one that matters. ⚠ **It is the other half of `SK3502`'s question, asked of a different declaration.** `SK3502` reads a *field* — the type constructs a disposable and offers no matching disposal — and says nothing about how the type cleans up; this reads a *method*, and says the cleanup exists and is unreachable. A type can be reported by both, and when it is, the two are saying different things: one that the resource is owned, one that the release is undeclared.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
sealed class Journal {
    readonly FileStream file = File.OpenWrite("journal");

    public void Dispose() {
        file.Dispose();
    }
}
```

Write:

```csharp
sealed class Journal : IDisposable {
    readonly FileStream file = File.OpenWrite("journal");

    public void Dispose() {
        file.Dispose();
    }
}
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **A `Dispose()` that was never meant to be the interface's is legitimate, and the two shapes of that are excluded by construction rather than by guesswork.** A `ref struct` is disposable through the language's pattern rule with no interface in sight, so its `Dispose()` *is* the contract — that is `SK3532`'s subject and it is skipped here. And a pooled object's `Dispose()` that returns the instance to its pool and clears its fields is not cleanup this rule can see: **the body must release something** — a `Dispose`, `DisposeAsync`, `Close` or `GC.SuppressFinalize` call — before the finding stands. That costs the rule every release routed through a helper it cannot name, and the cost is the right way round: the issue's rationale is "the type already wrote the cleanup", so where no cleanup is visible there is nothing to report. ⚠ **Not hosted, and that was measured rather than assumed.** `CA1063` and `CA1816` both take a type that *already* implements `IDisposable` as their subject, so neither can see one that does not; a probe built outside this repository with an empty `Directory.Build.props` above it produced no `CA` diagnostic of any severity — hidden included, read out of `-p:ErrorLog=` — on this shape at `AnalysisMode=All`. ⚠ A type implementing `IAsyncDisposable` is skipped: the disposal contract is declared, and whether it should also be synchronous is a design question. ⚠ An `override` of `Dispose()` is skipped, because the base is where the declaration is missing and reporting both says one thing twice. ⚠ Partial types are skipped — another part may carry the base list — and so is a type whose base type does not resolve, because `AllInterfaces` on an unresolved base is empty rather than unknown. ⚠ **The fix is `fixIsSafe: false` and the reason is not uncertainty about the edit.** Adding `IDisposable` widens a public surface: every caller may now wrap the type in a `using`, and every container will now tear it down at scope exit — which is the repair, and is still a behaviour change somebody should read. The edit itself is guarded twice: the interface is written qualified unless `IDisposable` already binds to `System.IDisposable` at the declaration's own position, and any directive in the header withdraws the finding, because the fix inserts at a position rather than replacing a node.
